lmarena_text_overall.intro: A widely recognised benchmark for how models feel in real use, designed to rule out the leaderboard gaming that fixed test sets allow.
lmarena_text_overall.method: Real users chat with two anonymous models at the same time, and the models are ranked by the users' actual votes.
lmarena_text_overall.cadence: High (results are recomputed daily to weekly as new user battles come in)

aa_intelligence_index.intro: An authoritative commercial reference for developers and businesses choosing models, showing overall value for money and practical deployment value at a glance.
aa_intelligence_index.method: Scores a model's intelligence, response speed and price together to produce a combined value-for-money index.
aa_intelligence_index.cadence: Medium (updated periodically as vendors release new model versions or change prices)

livebench_overall.intro: A hard test of a model's real problem-solving ability, built to stop models from scoring by memorising test questions.
livebench_overall.method: New questions are collected every month from recent sources (such as news or maths problems), so models cannot have memorised the answers in advance.
livebench_overall.cadence: Medium (new questions are released monthly and evaluations roll forward)

swe_bench_verified.intro: Widely regarded as the strictest benchmark for AI programmers, and the ultimate test of autonomous coding ability.
swe_bench_verified.method: The model is given a real bug from a real software project and must find the cause and fix the code on its own, as a human developer would.
swe_bench_verified.cadence: Low (the core task set changes slowly; the leaderboard rolls forward as new models are submitted)

deepswe.intro: A harder, deeper version of traditional code-repair tests, built to check senior, expert-level ability to fix bugs rooted in complex architecture or spanning several projects.
deepswe.method: The model is given a real failure in a large open-source project that involves several low-level dependencies or a large architecture, and must trace it to the root and fix it as a senior architect would.

frontiercode.intro: A research-level computer science exam that probes whether models can write cutting-edge, complex code that even human experts find hard.
frontiercode.method: Instead of routine business code or old contest problems, models tackle original programming problems in frontier research and highly complex low-level systems, where almost no ready-made reference answers exist.

mmlu_pro.intro: A much harder upgrade of MMLU, designed to squeeze out the lucky guesses that inflate models' scores on subject exams.
mmlu_pro.method: Each multiple-choice question gets more answer options, and many questions that need multi-step reasoning are mixed in, to tell real knowledge from guessing.
mmlu_pro.cadence: Low (a large static question bank, updated mainly when the maintainers replace or revise questions at scale)

gpqa_diamond.intro: A tough science exam that even PhD-level domain experts often get wrong, and a gold standard for a model's ability to assist research.
gpqa_diamond.method: PhDs in physics, biology, chemistry and other fields write the questions, testing whether models can answer highly specialised, obscure academic problems.
gpqa_diamond.cadence: Low (expert question-writing and cross-validation are very costly, so the question set grows slowly)

simpleqa_verified.intro: A lie detector for confident-sounding fabrication, and a core measure of whether a model's answers can be trusted.
simpleqa_verified.method: Asks factual questions that each have a single correct answer and wants the shortest possible reply (ideally one word), directly checking whether the model makes things up.
simpleqa_verified.cadence: Medium (a factual Q&A set can be topped up with long-tail knowledge relatively quickly)

humanitys_last_exam.intro: Billed as "Humanity's Last Exam", it is designed to find the limits and weak spots of today's strongest frontier models.
humanitys_last_exam.method: Collects extremely hard questions from top experts across many fields, aimed at stumping the AI models that already score near-perfectly on ordinary exams.
humanitys_last_exam.cadence: Low (the questions are very hard to collect, screen and verify, so releases are mostly static)

frontiermath.intro: A research-grade mathematics exam, and a touchstone for whether models can reach the frontier of human mathematics.
frontiermath.method: Models solve extremely hard problems that can take mathematics professors days of work, or that they may not crack at all; the final answers are checked exactly by machine.
frontiermath.cadence: Low (research-level problems are scarce and very hard to construct, so iterations are very slow)

arc_agi_2.intro: A pure test of generalising from a few examples rather than memorisation, widely regarded in the field as a key indicator on the path to true AGI (artificial general intelligence).
arc_agi_2.method: The model sees a few examples of colourful pattern transformations, works out the underlying rule as in a pattern-finding puzzle, and then produces the next pattern itself.
arc_agi_2.cadence: Low (it tests abstract logic and visual reasoning rather than knowledge, so it changes only with major official versions)

mmmu_pro.intro: A leading benchmark for solving hard specialist problems from images, and a core standard for university- to expert-level visual understanding.
mmmu_pro.method: The model is given the hardest illustrated exam questions from university subjects such as medicine, engineering and finance; it must read complex charts and diagrams and apply deep subject knowledge to solve them.
mmmu_pro.cadence: Low (collecting, reviewing and cross-checking expert-level illustrated questions is very costly; mostly released as static datasets)

videommmu.intro: A demanding test of whether models truly understand video, and one of the most advanced evaluations of long-video multimodal understanding.
videommmu.method: The model watches videos with specialist content (such as science experiments or lectures) and is tested not only on what it saw, but on whether it understands how events relate and change over time.
videommmu.cadence: Low (screening and manually annotating expert-level video Q&A data is a large effort, so updates are slow)

terminal_bench_4.intro: The leading test that simulates a real programmer's computer environment, and a core measure of whether terminal agents can actually take over computer work from people.
terminal_bench_4.method: The model is placed in a real command-line terminal and given a complex task; it must type commands, inspect files and debug code on its own to get the work done.
terminal_bench_4.cadence: Low (complex system-level sandboxes and automated grading scripts mean major versions are far apart)

bfcl_v4.intro: The industry's most authoritative leaderboard for calling external tools, which shows whether a model can act as the operational brain of complex business systems.
bfcl_v4.method: The model is given a set of APIs (such as weather lookup or flight booking) and long, complex user instructions, and must pick the right tools and fill in every parameter correctly.
bfcl_v4.cadence: Medium (the maintainers add test cases and re-score from time to time as major models update and real usage scenarios expand)

gaia.intro: A leading authority on how well general AI assistants (agents) solve real-world problems, exposing models that can talk but cannot act.
gaia.method: Poses complex everyday problems that require gathering information from several places over multiple steps, and checks whether the model can solve them fully on its own.
gaia.cadence: Low (building and manually verifying such multi-step, real-world tasks is very costly)

osworld.intro: The definitive test of whether a model can operate a computer as a person does, and a core standard for desktop AI assistants.
osworld.method: The model is placed in a real computer system and must click, type and use various applications in place of a person to complete the assigned work.
osworld.cadence: Low (virtual-machine setup and automated evaluation of complex interfaces make each iteration costly)

osworld_2.intro: A much harder upgrade of the computer-use test, built to challenge a model's stability and planning over long, multi-application work.
osworld_2.method: The model must switch back and forth between several applications to complete large, complex jobs that take a long time and many steps.
osworld_2.cadence: Low (building and sandbox-evaluating long system-level tasks is very complex; mostly static major-version updates)

longbench_v2.intro: One of the best-known comprehensive long-text benchmarks, measuring how well models handle, summarise and reason over large volumes of documents in real work.
longbench_v2.method: The model receives a large, disorganised pile of documents and must not only find information but also analyse and reason in depth across the long material.
longbench_v2.cadence: Low (cleaning and annotating high-quality long-text questions is very hard; depends on major official versions)

aa_scicode.intro: A benchmark in which models write code for real research problems in physics, chemistry, biology, mathematics and other fields. It is run uniformly by Artificial Analysis, so new models usually get results quickly.
aa_scicode.method: Each problem is split into subproblems; the model must write Python functions that pass the tests, and scoring is based on which subproblems pass.
aa_scicode.cadence: High (Artificial Analysis evaluates new models on a rolling basis as they are released)

aa_lcr.intro: An authoritative independent leaderboard for reasoning over very long text, showing how deeply models can analyse large volumes of material.
aa_lcr.method: The model receives very long articles or complex material; it is tested not only on remembering details but on complex reasoning that spans multiple passages.
aa_lcr.cadence: Medium (a third party re-evaluates periodically as vendors release long-context models)

graphwalks.intro: OpenAI's long-context reasoning benchmark, testing whether models can accurately track how nodes are connected across a large number of links.
graphwalks.method: The edges of a directed graph are listed in text; the model must find the nodes reachable at a given depth, or the parent nodes that point directly to a given node. This page uses the fixed BFS, 256K, F1 setting.
graphwalks.cadence: Irregular; updated with official data versions and published results.

chartography.intro: Surge AI's benchmark for understanding professional charts. Questions are written by professionals who use such charts in their work and reviewed by several experts, covering professional scenarios that common chart tests miss.
chartography.method: The model reads professional charts from fields such as medicine, finance and engineering, picks out key details, reads off the data, and calculates or reasons using domain rules.
chartography.cadence: Updated with official question-set versions and published results.

agents_last_exam.intro: An agent benchmark led by UC Berkeley RDI and other teams and built with industry experts, testing whether AI assistants can complete verifiable professional work.
agents_last_exam.method: The agent gets a clear task brief, input files and a software environment; it plans its own steps, uses tools and produces the deliverables, which a program then scores against hidden reference results. This page uses the full pass rate from the Overall leaderboard.
agents_last_exam.cadence: The question set rotates about every six months; scores update as new evaluations are submitted.

code_arena_webdev.intro: Real developers rate the web pages and front-end work that models build, to see whose results are more usable and better-looking.
code_arena_webdev.method: The same web development request goes to two anonymous models; users vote for the better result, and the votes are converted into an Elo ranking. It focuses on web and front-end work and is not a code-repair benchmark.
code_arena_webdev.cadence: High (updated continuously as votes come in)
